title: Four parts
hookLine: to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, one kept for hard times (DN 31)
carry: enjoy some, build with some, protect some

cards: Early morning near Rajagaha. A young man named Sigala stands with his clothes and hair still wet, bowing in six directions: east, south, west, north, down and up.
His dying father told him to, and he does it faithfully, without knowing why. The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks what he's doing.

Then, gently, he reinterprets the whole ritual: the six directions are the people in your life. What follows is a whole sutta of advice for ordinary life, and somewhere in the middle of it, there's a budget.

teach.b: East is your parents. South, your teachers. West, your spouse and children.
North, your friends. Below, those who work for you. Above, spiritual teachers.
For each, the Buddha lists what you owe them and what they owe you. Then, in a run of verses, he turns to money.

teach.h: LIKE A BEE, LIKE AN ANTHILL.
teach.b: The wise person gathers wealth the way a bee gathers nectar, a little at a time, and it grows the way an anthill grows. Then the budget: divide your wealth into four parts.

teach.h: ONE TO LIVE, TWO TO WORK, ONE TO KEEP.
teach.b: Live on one part and enjoy it. Put two parts to work in your business. Keep the fourth saved against hard times.

It would still make sense on a spreadsheet. Notice what it assumes: a householder will have money, should enjoy some, should invest in their livelihood, and should plan for misfortune. Nothing here is otherworldly.
The fractions don't map neatly onto a modern paycheck, and the tradition doesn't treat them as law; some read the two parts for work as money invested, others as the costs of running a trade.
The shape is the lesson: enjoy some, build with some, protect some, and decide on purpose.
The commentary, traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa, calls this sutta the discipline of the householder.
Monks have their rules. This is a lay person's.

how: The Sigalovada Sutta is widely taught to lay Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, as practical guidance for family, friendship, work and money.

s: Sigala was bowing to six directions because his father asked him to
it was his dying father's wish, and he kept it without knowing why.
the four-part budget tells the householder to give everything away
one part to live on, two for work, one saved for hard times.
the tradition treats the fractions as strict law

games.q: you're Sigala, still wet from bathing, bowing to six directions. the Buddha asks what you're doing. what does he do next?
o: tells you to stop the ritual.
reinterprets the six directions as your relationships.
games.why: in DN 31 he doesn't scold the ritual; he turns the six directions into parents, teachers, family, friends, workers and spiritual teachers.

practice: Without opening any app, picture your money in four piles, roughly as it is right now: the part you live on, the part that builds your work and your future, the part kept for hard times.
Don't calculate; just notice the shape, how it feels in the body to look at it, and whether one small adjustment suggests itself.

wordCard.voice: Four parts. The Buddha's advice to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, and one kept for hard times.

orig.note: Pali bhoga: wealth, possessions. DN 31's verse tells the householder to divide his wealth in four.

carryVoice: Your line: enjoy some, build with some, protect some. One for living, two for work, one for the rainy day. See you tomorrow.
